title: Voices in the Wild — Tactical Wishlist & Runtime Notes
summary: Working synthesis of recent customer threads (Aug–Sep 2026). Focus: runtime fragility, predictable fallbacks, small UX knobs with high perceived impact. Mix of raw quotes, quick priority mapping, and suggested next-step experiments for product/eng handoff.
body:
Purpose:
Capture a compact, testable set of asks and playbook steps surfaced in the last 6 weeks across EMEA and NA enterprise customers. Intention is to turn ‘noise’ into a small backlog of low-effort, high-confidence interventions we can A/B or pilot on Dedicated/Hosted tiers.

Field context (high level):
- Several customers are running mixed workloads (chat + embeddings) and report intermittent tail-latency spikes when autoscaling triggers and model routing falls back to smaller variants.
- Security-minded customers (finance / health) repeatedly ask for clearer signal when a private deploy is routing off-prem or when cached content might be served from shared nodes.
- A handful of early scale-ups ask for a lightweight ‘session pin’ control to force cold-starts to reuse warmed pools predictably for multi-user demos.

Representative customer quotes (anonymized):
- "We saw a 300ms bump every 3rd hour — it kills demo flow; we need a fallback indicator so the UI doesn't mislead."
- "Can we get an opt-in that says 'serve from dedicated pool' for specific routes?"
- "Token-level billing is great, but we can't reconcile spikes to requests without a mapped trace id in our logs."

Quick synthesis: problem clusters and heuristics
- Observability gaps: customers want traceable request -> cost/latency mapping and a visible 'service tier' flag in responses.
- Predictability controls: ability to pin routes to a pool (soft pin / hard pin), optionally warming on schedule.
- UX-level fallbacks: clear headers or minimal response metadata when model variant is degraded or capacity is constrained.

Tactical wishlist (prioritized for quick experiments):
1) Response-tier header (low effort): Add an X-RW-Serve-Tier header: hosted | dedicated | fallback. Gives customers immediate UI signal. Impact: high clarity, low infra change. Owner: CS -> propose to Platform.
2) Trace-id passthrough (medium): Inject a stable request_id propagated to logs + billing CSVs. Customers can correlate spikes. Requires small changes in Console and billing export. Owner: Observability.
3) Soft-pin route setting (medium): Route hint for customers to prefer a pool when available, but fall back if full. Polled TTL. Pilot with 3 customers. Owner: Dedicated product + infra.
4) Warm-schedule API (pilot): Endpoint to schedule warm-up for route/model combos (cron-like). Useful for demos & predictable peak windows. Consider quota/charge implications.
5) Fallback UX snippet (low): Return a short text flag in streaming responses (non-breaking) that client libraries can surface: e.g., "note: model_variant=fallback-small; latency_slo=best-effort".

Risk notes and non-starters (from customers):
- Hard guarantees on pinning without extra reserved capacity are unacceptable to customers; they prefer soft signals and explicit reserved contracts.
- Sensitive customers require that any additional response metadata not leak internal topology or IPs — keep headers opaque and documented.

Suggested experiment plan (next 6 weeks):
- Week 1: Implement X-RW-Serve-Tier header in hosted only; ship as beta flag. Create short release note and Slack channel.
- Week 2: Add request_id passthrough to logs and a sample billing-export mapping; onboard 2 pilot customers.
- Week 3–4: Build a small soft-pin prototype (route hint) behind a feature flag; test with staging clusters.
- Week 5–6: Offer warm-schedule API as opt-in pilot and measure cost delta and warm-up effectiveness.

Success metrics (initial):
- Reduction in demo-failure support tickets related to 'unexpected fallback' by >=40% for pilot customers.
- Customer satisfaction (post-pilot survey) >= 7/10 for predictability improvements.
- Observability: median time-to-correlate event->billing < 15 minutes for users using request_id.

Open questions for product/engineering: 
- How to encode tier header without exposing topology? (suggested encoding map in Confluence).
- Billing pipeline changes: can we augment historical exports without full re-ingest?
- Warm-schedule cost model: bill for warm-hours or include in burst-budget?

Action items (quick assignment):
- [Maya] Draft PRD stub for 'response-tier header' and 'request_id passthrough' by 2026-09-22.
- [Diego] Collect 3 concrete customer examples and latency traces for engineering by 2026-09-18.
- [Sana] Create short pilot onboarding checklist and consent language for private customers (privacy review) by 2026-09-23.
- [Owen] Run staging test of soft-pin route hint and report behavior on scale test by 2026-09-30.

Appendix: quick samples for UI teams (copyable):
- Header: X-RW-Serve-Tier: hosted
- Response snippet (streaming): {"rw_meta":"tier:dedicated,variant:rw-7b-q4"}  <-- prefer opaque single string in first pass

Notes to self: prioritize low-friction signals. Many customers will accept imperfect heuristics if they improve predictability for demos and core UX. Keep privacy team in loop for header metadata.
ask_items: Offer warm-schedule API pilot for demo-heavy customers
